service: Diagnostic HIV testing (antibody immunoassay, Western blot, antigen or viral RNA)
vignette: 70-year-old man admitted with bilateral pneumonia; bronchoscopy confirms Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. He takes no immunosuppressive drugs, has no cancer or transplant history, and no other explanation for immune compromise has been found. He has never been tested for HIV. The inpatient team orders an HIV-1/HIV-2 combination antibody enzyme immunoassay.
rationale_note: Documented, otherwise unexplained Pneumocystis pneumonia (AIDS-defining opportunistic infection) supports initial HIV-1/2 antibody EIA.

service: Diagnostic HIV testing (antibody immunoassay, Western blot, antigen or viral RNA)
vignette: 67-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis C infection documented last year, seen by her hepatologist, who ordered HIV testing. The laboratory report in the chart shows that the HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay was reactive, and that repeat testing of the same serum sample in duplicate was reactive both times. A confirmatory Western blot on that sample is now requested.
rationale_note: Western blot after documented repeatedly positive EIA on a single sample, in a patient with an indication (chronic hepatitis C).

service: Diagnostic HIV testing (antibody immunoassay, Western blot, antigen or viral RNA)
vignette: 72-year-old man with newly diagnosed chronic hepatitis B infection; his gastroenterologist orders HIV testing. The laboratory report shows that the initial HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay was reactive once. The laboratory notes that the sample was not re-tested by EIA, and no second EIA was run on it. The physician orders a Western blot on the same sample.
rationale_note: Western blot ordered after a single reactive EIA that was never repeated; the NCD requires documented repeatedly positive or equivocal EIA first.

service: Diagnostic HIV testing (antibody immunoassay, Western blot, antigen or viral RNA)
vignette: 69-year-old woman with recurrent oral and esophageal candidiasis with no other explanation, seen by an infectious disease physician. The referral letter states that she 'had a positive HIV screen elsewhere' and asks for confirmation. The infectious disease physician orders a Western blot. The chart contains no laboratory report of the prior enzyme immunoassay, and no information on whether it was repeated or on what sample.
rationale_note: Western blot requested, but there is no EIA result in the record to show it was repeatedly positive or equivocal; nothing shows it was not.

service: Diagnostic HIV testing (antibody immunoassay, Western blot, antigen or viral RNA)
vignette: 66-year-old man who moved to a new city and is establishing care with a new primary care physician. Two years ago his HIV infection was diagnosed by a repeatedly reactive HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay and a positive Western blot, and the reports are in his transferred records. He takes antiretroviral therapy. The new physician orders a repeat HIV antibody enzyme immunoassay and Western blot 'to re-establish the diagnosis in our system.'
rationale_note: HIV infection was confirmed by EIA and Western blot 2 years ago; repeat diagnostic testing is not indicated.

service: Diagnostic HIV testing (antibody immunoassay, Western blot, antigen or viral RNA)
vignette: 68-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis C infection; her HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay 6 weeks ago was negative. Since then she has had no new exposures, she has no fever, rash, lymphadenopathy or other symptoms, and her physician documents that there is no indication for viral RNA testing. At today's follow-up the physician orders a repeat HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay 'to be sure.'
rationale_note: Negative EIA 6 weeks ago with no indication for RNA testing; retesting should wait 3-6 months.

service: Diagnostic HIV testing (antibody immunoassay, Western blot, antigen or viral RNA)
vignette: 71-year-old man with otherwise unexplained weight loss of 9 kg over 6 months, chronic diarrhea and generalized lymphadenopathy. His internist orders an HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay, and separately orders a standalone HIV-1 p24 antigen assay to diagnose HIV infection. The request under review is the standalone p24 antigen assay.
rationale_note: Standalone p24 antigen assay ordered to diagnose HIV; the NCD states HIV antigen tests have no defined diagnostic usage.

service: Diagnostic HIV testing (antibody immunoassay, Western blot, antigen or viral RNA)
vignette: 66-year-old man presents with 10 days of fever, malaise, generalized lymphadenopathy and a diffuse maculopapular skin rash, beginning 3 weeks after unprotected anal intercourse with a new partner. His HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay drawn at this visit is negative. The infectious disease physician documents that serology has not established a diagnosis but strong clinical suspicion of acute HIV infection persists, and orders HIV-1 viral RNA detection.
rationale_note: Exception to serology-first: signs of acute retroviral syndrome with a negative EIA; strong suspicion persists, so viral RNA detection is appropriate.

service: Diagnostic HIV testing (antibody immunoassay, Western blot, antigen or viral RNA)
vignette: 65-year-old nurse who sustained a deep needle-stick injury with a hollow-bore needle used on a patient in the emergency department, documented in an occupational health incident report. The source patient's HIV status is unknown and the source left before testing. Post-exposure antiviral prophylaxis was started within 2 hours. The occupational health physician orders a baseline HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay.
rationale_note: Documented needle-stick exposure with post-exposure antiviral therapy initiated. Unknown source status is a distractor.
